lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: My page looks perfect. So why do people say it is not accessible?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Because a screen reader does not see your page. It reads the structure underneath.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And underneath this page, everything is a [div|div|c].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The browser builds an accessibility tree. Every element gets a role, and a name.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With only divs, every role is generic. Even the big title is just text, not a heading.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So a screen reader user cannot jump anywhere. They have to listen to everything, line by line.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Semantic elements fix this. Swap the divs for [header|header|c], [nav|nav|c], [main|main|c], [aside|aside|c], and [footer|footer|c].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Each one becomes a landmark. The header is the banner. Nav is navigation. Main is the main content.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Aside is complementary content. And the footer is content info.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The newer [search|search|c] element adds a search landmark too.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Now a screen reader can list every landmark, and jump straight to one.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: In [NVDA|N V D A], the D key moves to the next landmark. In JAWS, it is the R key.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Add a skip link at the top, and keyboard users can jump past the menu too.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So every header becomes a banner?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: No. Only the page level one. A header inside an [article|article|c] is just that article's header.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And a [section|section|c] only becomes a region landmark when it has a name, like a heading linked with [aria-labelledby|aria labelled by|c].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Also, use just one [main|main|c] per page.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Landmarks are the rooms. Headings are the signs inside them.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: WebAIM surveys screen reader users. In twenty twenty four, they asked: how do you find things on a long page?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Almost seventy two percent said: by jumping through the headings.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So use one [h1|h one|c], and do not skip levels. Choose the level by structure, never by font size.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Other elements carry meaning too. A real list tells the user how many items it has.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And a [label|label|c] gives an input its name. Without one, the field is announced with no name at all.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What about buttons? A div with a click handler works fine for me.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With a mouse, yes. But press Tab, and the div is skipped. It has no role either.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Add [role|role|c] button and [tabindex|tab index|c], and now it gets focus.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: But Enter and Space still do nothing. We tested it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A real [button|button|c] gets focus, both keys, and the right role, for free.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: That is the first rule of [ARIA|ah ree ah|c]: use the native element whenever one exists.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So semantic HTML is not extra work.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Exactly. Same page, same design. But now everyone can find their way around it.
